questions.qtext:
In a Go-Back-N (GBN) protocol, the sender uses a window size of $4$ and sequence numbers range from $0$ to $1023$ (modulo $1024$). Suppose the sender had transmitted packets with sequence numbers $500,501,502$, and $503$ , and $500$ was the base of the sender's window. After a while, the sender receives an ACK for packet $500$.

Assume:

  • The ACK is cumulative.
  • No other ACKs have been received.
  • No timeouts have occurred yet.


Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.text: The sender can now send packet $504$ immediately.
The sender must retransmit packet $500$, since no ACK for $501$ has been received.
The new sender window is [$501, 504$], and packets $501-503$ can be retransmitted if timeout occurs.
The base of the sender window remains unchanged until ACKs for all packets $500-503$ are received.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, C

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

Based on the principles of the Go-Back-N (GBN) protocol, the correct statements are A and C.

Here is the step-by-step breakdown of the logic:

1. Initial State

  • Window Size ($N$): 4

  • Transmitted Packets: $500, 501, 502, 503$

  • Sender Window: The window covers the sequence numbers of packets that have been sent but not yet acknowledged. Since $500$ is the base, the window is $[500, 501, 502, 503]$.

  • Window Capacity: The window is currently "full" (4 packets sent, 4 is the window size). The sender cannot send any new packets until the window slides.

2. The Event: "Receives an ACK for packet 500"

In the Go-Back-N protocol, acknowledgments are cumulative.

  • Receiving an "ACK for packet 500" means that packet $500$ has been successfully received and processed by the receiver.

  • This acknowledgment allows the sender to mark packet $500$ as "done" and slide the window forward.

3. The New State (After Sliding the Window)

  • Slide: The window slides one position to the right because the oldest packet ($500$) is acknowledged.

  • New Base: The new base becomes the next unacknowledged packet, which is $501$.

  • New Window Range: $[501, 501 + 4 - 1]$ = $[501, 504]$.

  • Packet Status:

    • $501, 502, 503$: These were already sent in the previous step and are now the "outstanding" packets inside the new window.

    • $504$: This sequence number has just entered the window. It has not been sent yet.

4. Evaluating the Options

  • A. The sender can now send packet 504 immediately.

    • CORRECT. Since the window slid to include $504$, and $504$ has not been transmitted yet, the sender is allowed to send it immediately.

  • B. The sender must retransmit packet 500, since no ACK for 501 has been received.

    • INCORRECT. Packet $500$ was acknowledged. There is no need to retransmit it. The absence of an ACK for $501$ just means $501$ is still pending; it does not trigger a retransmission of previous successful packets.

  • C. The new sender window is $[501, 504]$, and packets $501 - 503$ can be retransmitted if timeout occurs.

    • CORRECT.

      • The window is indeed $[501, 504]$.

      • In Go-Back-N, if a timeout occurs for the base packet (now $501$), the sender must retransmit all packets in the current window that have already been sent. Currently, those packets are $501, 502,$ and $503$.

  • D. The base of the sender window remains unchanged until ACKs for all packets $500 - 503$ are received.

    • INCORRECT. This describes a logic closer to a "Selective Repeat" variation or a misunderstanding of cumulative ACKs. In GBN, the window slides immediately as soon as the base packet ($500$) is acknowledged. It does not wait for the entire batch to clear.

Final Answer:

The correct statements are A and C.

Source solution 2 (score: 2)

What happens after ACK(500)?
--------------------------------
- New base = 501

- New window = [501, 502, 503, 504]

- Outstanding packets = 501, 502, 503 (not yet acked)

- One slot is free → sender *can* send 504 immediately

- ✅ This makes Option (1) true.

Timeout behavior in GBN
--------------------------------
- Timeout is always tied to the oldest unacked packet (the base).

- When base times out, **all outstanding packets (sent but unacked) starting from base** are retransmitted.

- Current base = 501 → if 501’s timer expires, retransmission starts from 501 onward.

Two cases for packet 504
--------------------------------
1. **504 is sent before timeout occurs**

- Outstanding = {501, 502, 503, 504}

- On timeout of 501 → retransmit {501, 502, 503, 504}

2. **504 is not sent before timeout occurs**

- Outstanding = {501, 502, 503}

- On timeout of 501 → retransmit {501, 502, 503}

Because of the word "can" in the option A we are considering case 2 for option (c).

I too made a mistake and only marked option (A) only 😅, but no worries — I learned something new. Hope this clears your doubt 🍀.

questions.qtext: In a sliding window protocol, the sender and receiver both use a window size of $N=5$. The sequence number space ranges from $0$ to $15$ . At a certain time, the sender's window includes the sequence numbers $0$ to $4$ , and the receiver's window includes the sequence numbers $2$ to $6$ . Which of the following best describes the current state?

options.text: The sender has received ACKs for packets $0$ and $1$ , and has sent packets $2$ to $4$.
The receiver is expecting packet $0$ , as it has not received any packets yet.
The sender has sent packets $0$ to $4$ , and packets $0$ and $1$ have been acknowledged.
The receiver has received packets $0$ to $2$ , and is waiting for $3$ to $7$ .

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 10)

Solution as per the position of the windows given.

Source solution 2 (score: 5)

  • The sender’s window is \([0,1,2,3,4]\). This means packets \(0\) and \(1\) have already been acknowledged, otherwise the sender’s window would have started earlier. Hence, the sender has sent packets \(0\) to \(4\), and ACKs for \(0\) and \(1\) are received.
  • The receiver’s window is \([2,3,4,5,6]\). This indicates that it has already received packets \(0\) and \(1\), and is now expecting packet \(2\) as the next in-order packet.

Thus, the correct description is that the sender has sent packets \(0\) to \(4\), and packets \(0\) and \(1\) have been acknowledged.

\[
\boxed{\text{Option C}}
\]

Source solution 3 (score: 2)

Answer: C. The sender has sent packets 0 to 4, and packets 0 and 1 have been acknowledged.

Reasoning: To solve this, we must look at the specific range of sequence numbers inside the windows for both the sender and the receiver.

1. Analyze the Sender's State:

  • Sender Window: [0,4] (Packets 0,1,2,3,4)

  • Meaning: The Sender window starts at 0. This means the sender has not yet received the acknowledgment (ACK) for packet 0. It is still waiting. The window is full (size 5), so the sender has likely sent all allowed packets (0 through 4).

2. Analyze the Receiver's State:

  • Receiver Window: [2,6] (Packets 2,3,4,5,6)

  • Meaning: The Receiver window starts at 2. This means the receiver has successfully received and processed packets 0 and 1. It has slid its window forward and is now waiting for packet 2.

3. Correlate the States (The "Gap"):

  • The receiver has moved past 0 and 1 (implying it sent ACKs for them).

  • The sender is still stuck at 0 (implying it hasn't received those ACKs yet).

  • This discrepancy is a standard "ACKs in flight" or "ACKs lost" scenario. The ACKs for 0 and 1 are currently traveling back to the sender or were lost.

4. Evaluate the Options:

  • A. (Incorrect) If the sender had received ACKs for 0 and 1, its window would start at 2, not 0.

  • B. (Incorrect) The receiver is not expecting 0; its window starts at 2, so it is expecting 2.

  • C. (Correct) The sender has utilized its window (sent 0-4). Packets 0 and 1 are "acknowledged" in the sense that the receiver has accepted them and sent the ACKs, creating the state where the receiver is ahead of the sender.

  • D. (Incorrect) The receiver is waiting for packet 2 (the base of its window). If it had already "received packets 0 to 2," its window would start at 3.

questions.qtext: Suppose it takes $1$ ms to send a packet, and the one-way propagation delay between the sender and receiver is $\mathbf{1 0} \mathbf{~ m s}$. The sliding window size is again $N=4$. What is the channel (or link) utilization?
questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

Correct Answer: A. 19.05%
Explanation:

  • Transmission time per packet $=1 \mathrm{~ms}$
  • One-way propagation delay $=10 \mathrm{~ms}$
  • Round-trip time $(\mathrm{RTT})=2 \times 10=20 \mathrm{~ms}$
  • Sliding window size $N=4$
  • Channel utilization $U$ is given by:

$$
U=\frac{N \times \text { Transmission Time }}{\text { RTT }+ \text { Transmission Time }}=\frac{4 \times 1}{20+1}=\frac{4}{21} \approx 0.1905=19.05 \%
$$

A sender is using a sliding window protocol with a window size of $4$ . It has sent packets $0$ to $3$ , and ACKs for packets $0,1,2$, and $3$ are currently propagating from the receiver to the sender. No ACK has yet been received by the sender. Assume cumulative ACKs are used and that the sender takes action only when an ACK is received or a timeout occurs.
Which of the following statements about the next possible event at the sender is/are correct?

options.text: If the next event is ACK1 (ACK0 was lost), the sender will slide the window and send packet $4$.
If the next event is ACK2 (ACK0 and ACK1 were lost), the sender will note that packet $2$ is ACKed but will not move the window or send any packet.
If the next event is ACK0, the sender will slide the window and send packet $4$.
If all ACKs (ACK0, ACK1, ACK2, and ACK3) are lost, the sender will receive a duplicate ACK for packet $3$ and move the window accordingly.

questions.solution:
Answer: A

What happens after ACK0?

- One slot is free → sender *can* send 4 immediately

In a Go-Back-N (GBN) protocol, the sender uses a window size of $4$, and sequence numbers range from $0$ to $1023$ (modulo $1024$). At a certain moment, the receiver is waiting for packet number $200$ to arrive in order.

Due to network propagation delay, some ACKs sent earlier by the receiver may still be in transit to the sender. Which of the following ranges correctly describes the possible ACK numbers that the sender may still receive at this point?
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 1)
  • Since the receiver is waiting for packet $200$, it has already acknowledged all packets up to $199$.
  • However, ACKs for earlier packets such as $196 to 199$ could still be propagating back due to delay.
  • These ACKs would still be valid and interpretable by the sender.
  • Hence, the possible ACK values seen by the sender could be in the range $196 to 199$.

A Go-Back-N protocol uses a window size of $5$ and cumulative acknowledgments. The parameters are as follows:

  • Timeout $=100 \mathrm{~ms}$, measured from the time the first bit of the packet is sent
  • Packet transmission time $=1 \mathrm{~ms}$
  • One-way link latency $=10 \mathrm{~ms}$


The sender begins transmitting packets $0$ to $4$ at $t=0$. All packets are received correctly except packet number $3$, which is lost.

When is packet $3$ first retransmitted (i.e., sent again after timeout expiry)?

options.text: $t=24 \mathrm{~ms}$
$t=102 \mathrm{~ms}$
$t=103 \mathrm{~ms}$
$t=100 \mathrm{~ms}$

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

Explanation:

At $t=0$, sender starts transmitting:

PacketSent at (ms)
00
11
22
33 (Lost)
44

Receiver side:

  • Packet $0$ reaches at $0+10=10 \mathrm{~ms} \rightarrow \mathrm{ACK}$ at $20$ ms
  • Packet $1 \rightarrow \mathrm{ACK}$ at $21$ ms
  • Packet $2 \rightarrow \mathrm{ACK}$ at $22$ ms
  • Packet $3$ is lost $\Rightarrow$ No ACK beyond packet $2$ is sent


Sender view:

  • ACKs for packets $0,1,2$ received by $t=22 \mathrm{~ms}$
  • No ACK for packet $3$ or beyond


Timeout:

  • Timeout for packet 3 starts at $t=3 \mathrm{~ms}$
  • Timeout expires at $3+100=103 \mathrm{~ms}$

At $t=103 \mathrm{~ms}$, the sender retransmits packet $3$. Since this is Go-Back-N, it will go back and retransmit packet $3$ and subsequent packets as needed.

Time Out starts for left most last oustanding packet in gbn ,for packet 3 it will start from 22 ms, so retranmission will be done at 22+100 i.e 122 ms

Source solution 3 (score: 1)
Question: When is packet 3 first retransmitted?

  • Parameters: Window=5, Timeout=100ms, $T_t=1$ms, $T_p=10$ms.

  • Events: Packets 0-4 sent at $t=0$. Packet 3 is lost.

Analysis:

  1. Sending Schedule:

    • $P_0$ starts at $t=0$. Ends $t=1$.

    • $P_1$ starts at $t=1$. Ends $t=2$.

    • $P_2$ starts at $t=2$. Ends $t=3$.

    • $P_3$ starts at $t=3$. Ends $t=4$. (This packet is lost).

    • $P_4$ starts at $t=4$. Ends $t=5$.

  2. Timeout Calculation:

    • The timeout is 100 ms, measured from the time the first bit of the packet is sent.

    • For Packet 3, the first bit is sent at $t=3$.

    • The timeout will expire at $3 + 100 = 103$ ms.

  3. Retransmission Logic:

    • In Go-Back-N, the sender waits for the timeout of the specific lost packet ($P_3$) to expire before resending it and all subsequent packets.

    • Therefore, the retransmission happens exactly when the timer expires.

Answer: C. $t = 103$ ms

questions.qtext:
A sender and receiver implement a sliding window protocol using selective retransmission with the following parameters:

  • Frame sequence number space: 0 to 4
  • Send window and receive window size: 2
  • One-way propagation delay: slightly less than 1 ms
  • Sender transmits one packet per ms
  • Timeout interval at sender: 4 ms
  • Receiver sends cumulative ACKs
  • ACK 1 is lost (as shown in the figure)
Figure: Sliding Window Timeline

Using the above setup and the timeline of packet exchanges shown, which of the following statements are correct?

Note: In this question, ACK n refers to the cumulative acknowledgment for Frame n, i.e., all frames up to and including Frame n have been received successfully.

options.text: The sender receives ACK 4 at t = 7 ms, confirming delivery of Frame 4.
Frame 0 is retransmitted at t = 6 ms, even though it was previously acknowledged.
ACK 1 is not retransmitted by the receiver after being lost.
Frame 2 is not retransmitted by the sender.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, C, D

Source solution 1 (score: 6)

The answer will be - A,C,D.

First, let me cover the confusing part -

Note: In this question, ACK n refers to the cumulative acknowledgment for Frame n, i.e., all frames up to and including Frame n have been received successfully.

This line does not make this system GB-N, which someone might think.

It just means that, if the sender recieves ACK2, the sender will assume packet 0,1 and 2 has been recieved. ACK1 need not be sent again. Getting ACK2 will itself means that packet 1 was reached and hence will also cover for the fact that ACK1 was sent but got lost. Please understand this correctly to avoid confusion which others are having.

Hence Option C is correct - Sender will recieve ACK2 at t=4 and assume packet 1 and 2 has reached. So the window size will go to 0-1-2-{3-4}. No ACK1 is retransmitted by the reciever, despite being lost.

Option A is correct -

At t=4, frame 3 will be sent, as soon as ack 2 is recieved.

At t=5, frame 4 will be sent. Tp=1 sec. At t=6 ( at reciever), frame 4 will reach receiver and ack will be sent and again tp=1, hence at t=7, frame 4 will be acknowledged.

At t=6 ( at sender ) - A new frame 0 will be sent (Difference between sent and retransmit). This is a new frame 0 and not the old frame 0 which was acknowledged before. Hence Option B is False

Option D is also correct since frame 2 was sent and acknowledgement and hence frame 2 won't be retransmitted.

If you have truly understood the concept regarding what I have written, you'll understand the fact that - Any frame will be retransmitted only if all ACK are lost during TOT of the frame.

at t=2 ms as ack 0 has been received hence the base of the window will shift and the window should be 1,2 .
